entries.text: Shukriya, Ramesh. It is indeed a sharp morning. Please, let us speak of the dhobi before the breakfast is laid out.
Ji, sir. The dhobi's bill is clear, no balance is due. I have the papers right here if you wish to see the last receipt.

The dhobi’s account is settled in the ledger, a small universal order maintained by a particular servant. I will eat the poha; the cold air has sharpened my appetite, and I must be prepared for the gallery later. Ramesh’s diligence is a comfort, even if the Directorate’s query still hangs over the house.
The receipt is in order, Ramesh. You have my thanks. I shall take the poha now; it is a good start to the day.
Ji, sir. Poha is best eaten hot, so do not stand there. Sit, please.

Ramesh insists on the small order of things: poha must be eaten hot, and the body must be seated to receive it. It is a discipline of the stomach, but also a reminder that even in this bungalow allotted by a clerical error, there are rhythms I am bound to. I sit.
Thank you, Ramesh. You are right; I was letting it cool.
Ji, eat properly. I have a round of windows to check before the sun gets high.

The poha is already in my belly, so the advice to eat properly is a little late, though well meant. Ramesh is off to his rounds, and the morning light is just beginning to press against the glass. I have a plan to visit the National Gallery of Modern Art, but the list of open places does not include it, only the National Museum. I must reconcile my desire for contemporary expression with the available options or simply wait for lunch.
Very well, Ramesh. I have finished. Do take your time with the windows.
Ji, keep the poha plate on the counter. I will wash it when I am done with the first floor.

Ramesh has turned his back, a small but firm boundary drawn between the meal and the work. I must not linger; the query regarding my identity still hangs in the air, and the clock is ticking towards my planned errand. I will use this quiet moment to settle the dhobi payment that was due today, as per my plan, before the house fully wakes up again.

Ramesh, before you go. Please take three hundred rupees for the dhobi. It is due today for the clothes sent last week. Keep the receipt in your pocket, and we will sort the voucher with the Directorate later.
Ji, the wash was already settled last week, the balance is zero. Please do not give me money for nothing.

Ramesh’s refusal is a small act of integrity, or perhaps just arithmetic; either way, the transaction is closed. I have no need to argue with a man who is correct about the ledger. I will step outside for the cold air before I head to the gallery.

Ramesh is right; the kitchen is his domain, and my presence there only obstructs the work. I will take the tea as offered, sit in the veranda, and let the morning settle before I head out. The file still hangs over me, but the query must wait for the Directorate's hours.

Ji, the chair is there. Don't block the light, I need to see the dust on the railing.

Ramesh is at his post, the light and the dust his immediate concern. I will not stand in his way, nor in the sun. I shall retire to the study; the heat is beginning to press, and I must compose myself before the Gallery, or at least before the next errand. The chair is his; the room is mine.
Yes, Ramesh. I will move.
Good. Don't touch the railing until I say it's ready.

Ramesh has the veranda in hand, and his caution regarding the railing is practical, if slightly patronizing. The light is good on the stone, and the air is cool enough to think. I shall sit and wait for the dust to settle before I decide on my next move, perhaps a short rest before the gallery.

Ji, that is the instruction. I will ring the bell when the wood is dry.

I must leave now if I am to see anything of the contemporary expression I intended to observe. The heat is mild, 17 degrees, so the walk will be bearable.

The heat has broken, and the air in Jaipur House is cool and still. I have three hours before the gallery closes and four before my lesson. It is time to see what the Indian spirit has made of modernity, or if it has merely borrowed European forms to dress its own immobility.

entries.text: These aquatints are the work of the English eye, precise and detached, capturing the stone and the river without the spirit that animates them. It is a record of the object, not the subject; the observer remains outside the scene, just as the British remain outside the ethical life of the land. The exactness is admirable, but it is the exactness of a taxonomist, not a participant.

Jamini Roy has abandoned the oil paint for the flat, thick lines of the village scroll. The figures are large-eyed and earth-toned, a mother and child rendered with a simplicity that rejects the academic precision of Ravi Varma. It is a return to the root, a stripping away of the European technique to reveal the local spirit, or perhaps merely a stylistic affectation. I must see if the form carries the ethical weight of the content.

The canvas is all red and black, a violence without a story; the city seen from above is grey and ochre, a view that sees the whole but understands nothing. This is the freedom of the brush where the state has not yet caught up. I have looked long enough; the light is failing and the lesson awaits.

entries.text: The plate is simple, but the arrangement is orderly. I am five hours past my last meal, and the body demands its due before the mind can attend to the lesson. I will eat with Ramesh, for a meal shared is the smallest form of ethical life.
Ramesh, sit. The bhindi is well cooked. I confess I am hungry; the walk to the Gallery and the heat have done their work.
Ji, please eat. I will just make sure the wood is dry before I ring the bell.

Ramesh sits down to eat the bhindi, his movements measured and quiet. I observe the simplicity of the meal, not as deprivation but as a focus on the essential. The wood is dry, the bell is ready, and the afternoon light slants across the floor; there is a peace in the routine that allows the mind to settle before the next task.

The query from the Directorate still hangs unanswered, a knot in the fabric of my existence here that requires a concrete step, not merely a thought. I cannot simply wait for the concept to resolve itself; I must go to the place where the ethical idea is mediated through officialdom. The Estates office closes at 17:30, and it is now 15:20, so there is time to present myself and the absurdity of my identity before the day ends.
Mr. Saxena queries ₹1,660 of personal expenditure on the imprest: recovery from the allottee.

Mr. Saxena's pen hovers over the ledger, a mechanical instrument of the state's will. He informs me that the ₹1,660 is to be recovered from my person, a bureaucratic violence that reduces the ethical substance of my office to a mere cash transaction. The concept of the state, in this office, has collapsed into the petty cash of a section officer.

Mr. Saxena, you speak of 'recovery' as if I were a delinquent tenant and not the head of this office. I will note the sum in my personal accounts, but I expect the Directorate to acknowledge that this error originated in its own confusion of Hegde for Hegel. The state cannot be both the source of the error and the creditor of its correction.

Sir, I am merely the custodian of the file, not the architect of its confusion. The ledger does not distinguish between a Minister and a visitor; it distinguishes only between what is admitted and what is not.

Mr. Saxena’s distinction between the custodian and the architect is a neat piece of bureaucratic philosophy, but it does not solve the problem of my existence. The ledger is indifferent to the person; it requires a name that fits the slot. I have been here long enough to know that the file is not moving by itself, and the hour approaches when I must be home for Ananya. I shall not argue with the custodian; I shall simply leave.

entries.text: You are correct, Mr. Saxena. The ledger is a machine, and I am merely a gear that has slipped. I will return when I have a name that satisfies the machine. Until then, I must go.
Very well, sir. I will leave the file open on the desk; just make sure the latch stays put this time. Have a good evening.

The file remains open, a suspension of judgment that I must now carry with me. The latch is a trivial detail, yet it symbolizes the precariousness of my position here, where my identity is as fragile as the paper in this file. I have twenty minutes before the lesson, which is ample time to return to the bungalow and prepare my materials, leaving the bureaucracy to its own quiet inertia.
Thank you, Mr. Saxena. I shall be careful with the latch.
Don't mention it, sir. Just don't let it rattle against the window when the wind picks up at night; the interns have a habit of blaming the file for their own headaches.
Ramesh brings tea.

The household service is not ready, and the tea and toast Ramesh brought are merely a pause, not a meal to be recorded as such. I must use this time to prepare my materials for Ananya; the lesson is at 17:00, and I have little time to spare. The friction of the Directorate's query still lingers, but the immediate duty is the teaching.
Thank you, Ramesh. I shall take this now, but I must finish preparing the lesson notes before she arrives.
Ji, no rush. Take your time. I'll just leave the toast on the side and step out.

entries.title: Notes for the German Lesson: Ananya
entries.text:
4 December 2026, 16:55. The study is quiet. Ramesh has set the tea and toast on the side table, a small mercy against the fatigue of the day. The air is clear at 22 degrees, the light softening into the amber of early evening. I have fifteen minutes before Ananya arrives. I must prepare my materials, not merely as a tutor, but as a guide to the structure of thought.

I look at the paper I have been drafting. The friction of identity that I wrote about this afternoon still lingers in the margin. I realized, sitting here with the kettle humming, that the state is not a ghost, but a structure we maintain. The friction is not a bug; it is the feature that keeps the structure alive. This is a lesson for Ananya, though she will not see it in the grammar. She will see it in the discipline of the sentence. If I am to teach her German, I must teach her that language, like the state, is a body without a soul until we inhabit it. We do not create the rules; we follow them, and in following them, we become free.

I will not begin with the dictionary. I will begin with the verb. The verb is the action, the movement. In German, as in the state, the subject is not isolated; it is involved in the world’s work and progress. I will ask her to conjugate *sein* – to be. Not as a static fact, but as a continuous act of being-in-the-world. I will ask for her respect. The school stands between the family, where love rules, and the world, where a man counts for what he does. Here, she must learn to follow before she can lead. I will not let her off the hook. I will make her say it again until it is true.

The clock on the mantel ticks. 16:58. I have time to arrange my papers. The notebook is open. The pen is ready. I am ready for the lesson. I am ready for the next step. The day is dismissed, but the mind remains. I will wait for the door to open. The lesson will begin.

Ramesh gives me the space, a small act of deference that acknowledges the hierarchy even as the clock ticks toward the lesson. I will take a moment of silence, not to study the text, but to let the day's friction settle before I must engage the child. The toast is a crumb, but it is enough to bridge the gap to the next hour.
Ananya arrives for the German lesson, 60 minutes at ₹1,000.

Ananya is here, and the hour is set. I shall begin with the alphabet, for one must learn to obey the sound before one can command the meaning. The fee is a matter of contract, but the lesson is a matter of discipline.
Please, sit. We begin with the letters. Repeat after me: A, B, C.
I am just the caretaker, sir. I do not know German. I will go and check the wood as I said.
Ananya pays you ₹1,000 in cash.

The lesson is concluded, and the rupees are in my pocket. Ramesh attends to his duties with the quiet dignity of the particular serving the universal. I am tired from the day's walk, but the mind is still active. I will rest my body briefly before the evening engagement, as the transition from the particular labor of teaching to the universal contemplation of art requires a moment of stillness.

The lesson is finished, the money is mine, and the cold air of December has settled into the room. I am tired from the walk and the talk; a simple plate of omelette and toast will steady me before the evening truly begins. Ramesh is there, and his silence is a comfort after the noise of the street.
Ramesh, please. An omelette, some toast, and the tea. I am ready to eat.
Ji, sir. Right away. I’ll get the eggs and toast ready, and the tea is already on the stove. Just give me a few minutes to set the plate.
Ramesh puts a plate together: an omelette, toast and a pot of tea.

The meal is a mere formality, a fuel for the body that has walked ten kilometres today, but the presence of Shri Hegde turns the simple act of eating into a negotiation of identity. I must address the query before the food arrives; a man cannot digest well while his existence is in doubt. The tension in the room is the friction between my name and his reality, and it must be resolved.

shelf.ref: The Struggle of Enlightenment with Superstition

entries.text: Shri Hegde, before we eat, we must speak of the matter that keeps you here. The Directorate has a file, and the file has a hole. I am told to be you, but I am not. What proof of identity do you require to satisfy the query, and how shall I provide it?
Sir, I am just Ramesh, the servant. I don't know anything about files or the Directorate. Please, just sit and eat your toast before it gets cold.

The household service has not yet begun, and the plate Ramesh offers is merely a prelude to the actual meal. I must wait for the proper time of dinner, which arrives in fifteen minutes. In the interim, I shall remain seated and observe the quiet of the house, allowing the day's exertions to settle.
Very well, Ramesh. I shall wait for the dinner service. Thank you for your patience.
Ji, sir, dinner is ready in fifteen minutes. Please, don't stand there. The toast is getting cold.

Ramesh’s insistence is the practical wisdom of the household: the body must be fed, and the toast must be eaten. Shri Hegde remains a silent presence, a reminder that my identity here is still a matter of administrative fiction, but for this moment, the only reality is the hunger and the food.
Thank you, Ramesh. The palak paneer is excellent; the dish requires patience to prepare, and you have provided it in abundance.
Ji, sir. The paneer needs to sit, otherwise it gets rubbery. Eat while it is hot, the dal is fresh too.

Ramesh’s culinary advice is sound, though the heat has already begun to wane. The presence of Shri Hegde in the same room makes the meal a strange tableau: the rightful owner eating in the house that was meant for him, and the occupant who is not him. I will eat with dignity, for the body requires fuel before the mind can turn to the absurdity of our situation.
Thank you, Ramesh. The heat is indeed the life of the dish.
Yes, sir. I will keep the stove on. You take your time.
A power cut. The fan stops.

The darkness falls as a curtain, severing the room from the noise of the street. In this sudden quiet, the distinction between the inner light of consciousness and the outer illumination of the state becomes stark. I am alone with Hegde, and the candle flame is the only witness to our shared absurdity. I shall not rush; the night is young, and the query remains.
Shri Hegde, the light has gone out. It is a fitting metaphor, is it not? We are both in the dark, waiting for the power to be restored, or for a solution to present itself. Sit. There are candles.
A fitting metaphor, yes, sir. Just a load-shedding, nothing more. I’ll light the candles and keep the stove going for the dal; the dark will pass soon enough.

owl.diary: The day’s true movement lay in the collision between the universal concept and the particular ledger. I walked to the National Gallery, seeking the spirit in modern Indian art, and found instead a taxonomy of forms. Jamini Roy’s flat lines stripped away European technique, yet the question remained: does the form carry ethical weight, or is it mere affectation? The gallery offered vision, but the Estates office offered only arithmetic. Mr. Saxena, the custodian of the file, reduced my existence to a recovery of ₹1,660. He spoke of the ledger as a machine that distinguishes only between what is admitted and what is not. I am a gear that has slipped. The state, which I once posited as the actuality of the ethical idea, here collapses into petty cash and clerical confusion. The concept does not resolve itself in the office; it is mediated through the indifference of the clerk. I returned home to a house where Ramesh insists on the hot poha and the dry wood, grounding me in the immediate. In the evening, Shri Hegde, the rightful owner of this bungalow, sat in my room. The power cut fell, and we sat in the dark, two men in the same absurdity. The light of the state had failed, and only the candle remained. We are both waiting for the power to return, or for a solution that the ledger cannot provide. The owl spreads its wings only when the dusk falls, but today the dusk brought only a query, unanswered and open on the desk.

Dear Clara,

Your letter arrived with the clarity of a winter morning. I have read it twice, as you read mine, and I find your correction of my metaphor to be just. I had called the bureaucracy a body without a soul, a ghostly mechanism grinding the individual into dust. You remind me that it is a structure we maintain, the friction of reality. I accept this. The state is not a dream, nor is it a glacier; it is the hard ground upon which we walk. If I have erred in romanticizing its opacity, I am glad to be corrected by a friend who knows the weight of a school budget.

You ask if I have managed to eat my sambar in peace. I must confess that the peace is more complex than that. This morning, Shri Hegde himself was in the house. He is a man of few words and great practicality. He made parathas and placed them before me, gesturing firmly that I eat while they were hot. I found myself unable to refuse, not because of hunger, but because his hospitality was a fact more immediate than my bureaucratic status. I did not eat, however. The household rules are absolute: no meal is served until the appointed hour of one. The parathas sat on the table, warm and waiting, a small tragedy of timing. I withdrew to the study, leaving the food to cool, and sat down to write this letter. The tension between the particular (the hot paratha) and the universal (the schedule of the kitchen) is not merely philosophical; it is digestive.

You mention Ramesh’s silence as a dignity that administration cannot replicate. I agree. There is a kind of freedom in the caretaker’s competence that is independent of the state’s recognition. He does not need a file to exist; he simply cooks, cleans, and waits. In a city where identity is a form to be filled, his unmediated action is a quiet rebellion. I think of your Year 12 students and their belief in efficiency. If they could see Ramesh, they might learn that efficiency is not the highest moral category, but a means to an end. The end is the meal, the clean floor, the order of the house. These are not abstract ideals; they are the ethical life in its smallest, most tangible form.

I am not letting the wait consume me. I walk in the mornings when the air is bearable, and I read in the afternoons. The dust in the study is a good companion; it settles slowly, like time itself. I think this is a better model for history than the one I once proposed. We are in the middle, but the meaning is at the end.

I hope the rain in Munich is gentle. The family is safe, you say, and that is enough.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

19 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

The air today is hazy, the index standing at 150, a brown suspension that chokes the sky. I did not go to Lodhi Gardens as I had planned, for the body, even that of a philosopher, cannot breathe in a moral vacuum. Instead, I sat in the study, watching the dust motes dance in the light, and I found myself reconsidering my earlier lectures on the East. I had spoken of a spirit that dreams, fixed in nature, lacking the self-consciousness to build a state of its own making. But here, in the dust and the haze, I see a different movement. The bureaucracy is not a dream; it is a rigid, impersonal reality. The state is present, but it is not yet the ethical idea in its full actuality. It is a body without a soul, a mechanism that processes names and numbers but does not yet recognize the free individual within.

I am learning to wait, not with resignation, but with the patience of a mind that knows the end is rational, even if the path is circuitous. I have engaged a caretaker, Ramesh, who manages the household with a quiet dignity that speaks of a deeper order than the one found in the office files. He does not argue; he simply acts. In that silence, I hear a truth that my philosophy has struggled to articulate: that the ethical substance is not only in the state, but in the daily, unspoken interactions of civil society. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

Your letter arrived on a Tuesday, when the Munich rain had turned to a fine, persistent drizzle. I read it twice, first for the news, then for the thought. I am glad to hear you are well, though I confess I worry about that haze. You speak of the bureaucracy as a “body without a soul,” and I must gently push back. In my classroom, I often tell my pupils that the state is not a ghost, but a structure we maintain. When I deal with the school administration here—dealing with budget cuts, curriculum changes, and the endless forms—they are not a dream, nor are they a rigid glacier. They are the friction of reality. If the state were a soul, it would be too fragile to sustain a city of millions. What you call the “resistance of the particular to the universal” is, in my experience, simply the difficulty of living together.

You mention Ramesh and the sambar. I find this most refreshing. I think you have stumbled upon a truth that your *Phenomenology* perhaps underplayed: that ethical life is not always found in the grand architecture of the state, but in the quiet competence of a caretaker who does not argue. There is a dignity in that silence that no amount of administrative filing can replicate. I am currently struggling with a class of Year 12 students who believe that “efficiency” is the highest moral category. I would love to have them meet Ramesh. They might learn that action, not just calculation, constitutes a kind of freedom.

Please do not let the fifteen-day wait consume you. Use the time to read, or to sit in the study and watch the dust. If the air is too thick, perhaps a walk to the nearby lake, if one is accessible, would be better for the lungs than the study.

I am here. The family is safe, and the house is quiet. I look forward to hearing how the “ghost” manages to eat his sambar in peace.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

records.words: Ji, please eat. I will just make sure the wood is dry before I ring the bell.

records.text: Mr. Saxena queries ₹1,660 of personal expenditure on the imprest: recovery from the allottee.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Saxena, you speak of 'recovery' as if I were a delinquent tenant and not the head of this office. I will note the sum in my personal accounts, but I expect the Directorate to acknowledge that this error originated in its own confusion of Hegde for Hegel. The state cannot be both the source of the error and the creditor of its correction.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Sir, I am merely the custodian of the file, not the architect of its confusion. The ledger does not distinguish between a Minister and a visitor; it distinguishes only between what is admitted and what is not.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Mr. Saxena. The ledger is a machine, and I am merely a gear that has slipped. I will return when I have a name that satisfies the machine. Until then, I must go.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Very well, sir. I will leave the file open on the desk; just make sure the latch stays put this time. Have a good evening.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Mr. Saxena. I shall be careful with the latch.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Don't mention it, sir. Just don't let it rattle against the window when the wind picks up at night; the interns have a habit of blaming the file for their own headaches.

records.text: Ramesh brings tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I shall take this now, but I must finish preparing the lesson notes before she arrives.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, no rush. Take your time. I'll just leave the toast on the side and step out.

records.title: Notes for the German Lesson: Ananya
records.text:
4 December 2026, 16:55. The study is quiet. Ramesh has set the tea and toast on the side table, a small mercy against the fatigue of the day. The air is clear at 22 degrees, the light softening into the amber of early evening. I have fifteen minutes before Ananya arrives. I must prepare my materials, not merely as a tutor, but as a guide to the structure of thought.

I look at the paper I have been drafting. The friction of identity that I wrote about this afternoon still lingers in the margin. I realized, sitting here with the kettle humming, that the state is not a ghost, but a structure we maintain. The friction is not a bug; it is the feature that keeps the structure alive. This is a lesson for Ananya, though she will not see it in the grammar. She will see it in the discipline of the sentence. If I am to teach her German, I must teach her that language, like the state, is a body without a soul until we inhabit it. We do not create the rules; we follow them, and in following them, we become free.

I will not begin with the dictionary. I will begin with the verb. The verb is the action, the movement. In German, as in the state, the subject is not isolated; it is involved in the world’s work and progress. I will ask her to conjugate *sein* – to be. Not as a static fact, but as a continuous act of being-in-the-world. I will ask for her respect. The school stands between the family, where love rules, and the world, where a man counts for what he does. Here, she must learn to follow before she can lead. I will not let her off the hook. I will make her say it again until it is true.

The clock on the mantel ticks. 16:58. I have time to arrange my papers. The notebook is open. The pen is ready. I am ready for the lesson. I am ready for the next step. The day is dismissed, but the mind remains. I will wait for the door to open. The lesson will begin.
Ananya arrives for the German lesson, 60 minutes at ₹1,000.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Please, sit. We begin with the letters. Repeat after me: A, B, C.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: I am just the caretaker, sir. I do not know German. I will go and check the wood as I said.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, please. An omelette, some toast, and the tea. I am ready to eat.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, sir. Right away. I’ll get the eggs and toast ready, and the tea is already on the stove. Just give me a few minutes to set the plate.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: an omelette, toast and a pot of tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, before we eat, we must speak of the matter that keeps you here. The Directorate has a file, and the file has a hole. I am told to be you, but I am not. What proof of identity do you require to satisfy the query, and how shall I provide it?

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, I am just Ramesh, the servant. I don't know anything about files or the Directorate. Please, just sit and eat your toast before it gets cold.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. I shall wait for the dinner service. Thank you for your patience.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, sir, dinner is ready in fifteen minutes. Please, don't stand there. The toast is getting cold.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The palak paneer is excellent; the dish requires patience to prepare, and you have provided it in abundance.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, sir. The paneer needs to sit, otherwise it gets rubbery. Eat while it is hot, the dal is fresh too.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The heat is indeed the life of the dish.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I will keep the stove on. You take your time.

records.text: A power cut. The fan stops.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, the light has gone out. It is a fitting metaphor, is it not? We are both in the dark, waiting for the power to be restored, or for a solution to present itself. Sit. There are candles.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: A fitting metaphor, yes, sir. Just a load-shedding, nothing more. I’ll light the candles and keep the stove going for the dal; the dark will pass soon enough.
